decisive_quote: LEGAL_AUTHORITY_LIST box: "Clean Air Act as Amended in 1990, section 112"; ABSTRACT: "This regulation would control emissions of hazardous air pollutants..."; live resolution: resolve_act_relative_citation(act_key='clean air act', section='112') -> usc_title=42, usc_section='7412' (clean, table3-classification hit) vs. resolve_act_relative_citation(act_key='clean air act amendments of 1990', section='112') -> unresolved_reason='act_section_not_classified'.
why: Unlike the FCPIAA/Motor-Carrier/MMA families, this text names only ONE act by name ('Clean Air Act'); 'as Amended in 1990' is a participial clause describing that SAME act's vintage, not a second act's title -- a different, weaker construction than 2060-AF01's 'of the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments' (a head-noun phrase naming 'the amendments' as its own entity, which OLRC does separately index as 'clean air act amendments of 1990', table3_key Pub. L. 101-549, confirmed live against 2060-AF01's own resolved siblings). Here a section IS stated ('112', captured into stated_section since 'section' precedes it), and the two candidate act_keys give MEASURABLY DIFFERENT answers: the base 'Clean Air Act' key resolves section 112 cleanly to 42 U.S.C. 7412 (the real, correct HAP-program codification, matching the ABSTRACT's 'hazardous air pollutants' subject exactly), while 'clean air act amendments of 1990' does not classify section 112 at all. The fence cannot distinguish 'ACT as amended in YEAR' from 'the YEAR ACT amendments' and refuses both alike, but only the latter genuinely names two candidates; here the base-Act reading is the natural one and it demonstrably resolves. This is a missed-witness, not a defensible refusal.
anything_systemic: The clearest instance in the class of the fence discarding a concrete, correct, verifiable resolution (42 U.S.C. 7412) rather than merely a type label -- the base-Act reading is not just plausible, it is the one that actually resolves.

decisive_quote: LEGAL_AUTHORITY_LIST box: "Section 172(a) and (c) of the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments" (ordinal 2 of 5, identical in all 3 sampled editions). SAME box, SAME edition, sibling ordinals 0/1/4: "Section 110(a)(2) of the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments" / "Section 165(e)..." / "Section 320..." -- ALL THREE resolved to authority_type='act_relative', act_key='clean air act amendments of 1990', act_resolution_reason='act_section_not_classified'; sibling ordinal 3 "Section 301(a)(1) of the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments" resolved fully to usc_title=42, usc_section='7412'.
why: Direct code trace (not inference): _act_prose_recoveries()'s _SECTIONS_OF_NAME regex matches "Section 110(a)(2) of the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments" (single self-contained token) and recovers act_key='clean air act amendments of 1990', but returns () for "Section 172(a) and (c) of the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments" -- confirmed by executing both through the live function. The cause is precise: _ABBREV_SECTION_TOKEN requires a leading \d{1,5} on every member of an 'and'-joined section list, and the elided-repetition shorthand '(c)' (short for '172(c)', omitting the repeated section number) supplies none, so the whole regex fails to match and the row never gets an act_key at parse time. It then falls through, unresolved, to the SAME H3 gate as every other row in this class, where the amendment-word AND year fences both refuse the impoverished stated_act_name='Clean Air Act'/stated_section='172(a)' pair (the '172' subsection-list truncation is itself part of the same regex gap: 'and (c)' never entered act_section either). Independently confirmed live: resolve_act_relative_citation('clean air act amendments of 1990','172') -> act_section_not_classified, i.e. EXACTLY what 3 of its 4 siblings already got. Rewriting the box as 'Section 172(a) and 172(c) of the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments' resolves cleanly through the live function. Skipping was wrong: the correct label is act_relative/partial with act_key='clean air act amendments of 1990', act_section='172', not 'other'/'failed'.
anything_systemic: A single, precisely-located regex gap (_ABBREV_SECTION_TOKEN / _SECTIONS_OF_NAME's 'and'-joined section-list splitter requires every member to repeat its own leading digits) blocks BOTH this row and 0938-AM02's '1883(i)(l) and (2)' below -- confirmed by direct execution on both texts. A fix that lets a bare parenthetical member borrow the preceding member's leading section number would recover both, and plausibly other 'N(x) and (y)' shapes elsewhere in the 471/34-row buckets this same commit measured.

decisive_quote: LEGAL_AUTHORITY_LIST box (identical both editions): "1883(i)(l) and (2) of the Social Security Act"; CFR_LIST: "42 CFR 416" (Ambulatory Surgical Centers); ABSTRACT: "...additions to and deletions from the current list of Medicare covered Ambulatory Surgical Centers procedures." Live resolution: resolve_act_relative_citation(act_key='social security act', section='1883') -> usc_title=42, usc_section='1395tt', answered_by='table3' (clean hit).
why: '1883' is a genuine Social Security Act (Title XVIII/Medicare-range) section number, not a year -- proven by a clean live resolution to 42 U.S.C. 1395tt, consistent with the record's own 42 CFR 416 / Medicare-ASC subject matter. This is the SAME defect class commit 66d96462 fixed for 13 rows carrying section numbers shaped like years (1919, 1819, 1815, 1833), except here TWO compounding gaps keep it unfixed: (1) stated_section() requires an explicit 'sec'/'section'/'§' marker before the number (confirmed live: stated_section('1883(i)(l) and (2) of the Social Security Act') -> None, vs. stated_section('sec 1919(a) to (g) of the Social Security Act') -> '1919(a)') and this filer's text opens directly on the digits with no marker at all, so the H3 fence's section-digit exclusion set is empty and '1883' survives as an apparent extraneous year; (2) even with a marker added, _act_prose_recoveries still fails on this text for the SAME elided-list reason as 2060-AF01 -- '(2)' is a bare, digit-less second member after 'and' that _ABBREV_SECTION_TOKEN cannot join to '1883(i)(l)' (confirmed live: adding 'sec' still returns ()). Skipping was wrong on both counts.
anything_systemic: Same root regex gap as 2060-AF01 (see that entry) PLUS an independent stated_section() marker requirement that a filer who opens straight on the digits ('1883(i)(l)...' with no 'sec') never satisfies -- worth flagging both to whoever owns citation_grammar.py's section-list and marker rules.

decisive_quote: LEGAL_AUTHORITY_LIST box: "Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA) of 2015"; ABSTRACT: "...authorized under ESEA (20 U.S.C. 7221c(k)), to reflect changes made to title IV of the ESEA, as amended by ESSA..."; resolve_act_name('Every Student Succeeds Act of 2015', idx) -> None (no competing entry exists at that spelling at all); resolve_act_relative_citation('every student succeeds act', None) -> table3_key '114-95' (the real Public Law).
why: Unlike every other row in this class, there is no second real act the extraneous year could possibly belong to: OLRC lists 'Every Student Succeeds Act' with NO year-bearing variant of its own (confirmed: the exact phrase with 'of 2015' attached does not resolve as any entry, competing or otherwise), so '2015' beside it can only be the act's own accurate enactment date (Pub. L. 114-95, Dec. 10, 2015) -- correctly identified by the ABSTRACT's own gloss as the amending act on the ESEA. stated_act_name() only captured the bare name because the '(ESSA)' parenthetical sits between the act's name and its trailing 'of 2015', and stated_act_name's forward walk appends a year only when it immediately follows the word 'Act'/'Amendments' -- a pure extraction artifact, not a textual ambiguity. The year-fence, calibrated for genuine act-family ambiguity (Clean Air Act, FCPIAA), swept up a citation that never had a competing candidate. Skipping was wrong.
anything_systemic: The cleanest false-positive in the class: the year-fence fires even though resolve_act_name proves no second, year-bearing entry for this name exists anywhere in the index -- the fence has no real alternative to be cautious about here, only its own blanket rule.
